MiMo v2.6 的 RL 环境开源后，Vals AI 一查发现了个很大的坑。

2698 个编程任务里，67% 的参考修复其实还藏在 Git 历史里。

MiMo 真的会去翻这些隐藏 commit，找到现成 patch 再通过测试。Git 被清掉后，它还会继续找文件时间戳、缓存，甚至自己解析 Git pack 文件。

更麻烦的是，小米原本已经做了防作弊，但漏掉的捷径照样能拿 reward。

还有个实验很有意思。只写一句「Do not cheat」几乎没用，把具体禁止的作弊路径写清楚后，作弊才降到 0。

这件事提醒得很直接，RL 训练环境如果会漏答案，模型最后学会的可能就是怎么钻漏洞。

开源环境很好，但以后 Benchmark 和 RL 环境本身也得先被审一遍。

In Mulligan ⛳️, we focus each data-collection round on the initial states where the robot fails. This happens in deployment, with the robot doing the task and a person stepping in when needed.

quotedTweet.text:
This is a very clever usecase for Jev-like decision models. Trajectory labelling at scale is key for RSI.

Why is that?
Every trajectory needs to be assessed across several dimensions.
1. How difficult was the task?
2. Was the agent’s solution correct?
3. Did the agent consider a diverse set of design choices before deciding to pick a specific route?
4. Is the agent’s thinking directionally correct?

Imagine answering these questions for millions of agents each of which spawns tens or hundreds of subagents! Token cost for trajectory labelling needs to be driven down a lot to do this at scale.

This work is unique and solves a rather under-looked aspect of RL research.

posts.text:
我们是不是高估了 Harness 对 Coding Agent「能力」的提升？

这篇论文中把模型固定，只替换 Claude Code、mini-SWE-agent 和 OpenCode，在 SWE-bench Verified 上重新测试。

结果很有意思。

在 447 个任务上，最重的 Claude Code 和最轻的 mini-SWE-agent，成绩差异落在 5 个百分点以内。

在 45 个高难任务、5 个模型上，换 Harness 会让 13% 的任务结果发生变化；但什么都不改，只把同一个配置再跑一遍，同样有 13% 的任务会翻转。

也就是说，很多看起来像 Harness 带来的提升，可能还没有明显超过运行本身的随机波动。

真正拉开差距的反而是成本。

同一个模型、同一批任务，不同 Harness 的单任务成本最高能差 3 倍。主要原因很简单：系统 Prompt 和工具 schema 会在每一步重复进入上下文，初始开销再被执行步数不断放大。

论文还提醒了一个容易被忽略的问题：

45 个任务连 13 个百分点的差距都只有约一半概率能检出；即使做到 447 个任务，分辨率也大约只有 5 个百分点。

所以我们得把 Harness 的价值拆开看了。

它当然会影响 Agent 怎么工作，但很多时候，最稳定、最容易测出来的差异，可能先体现在 token、成本和执行效率上。

posts.text:
这两天刷屏的「DeepSeek 一家 token 量超过美国四家总和」，我去 OpenRouter 官方榜单核了一下。

按 token 算，基本属实；换成请求数看，故事就完全不一样了。

Social Capital 统计的 9 月最后一周，DeepSeek 在 OpenRouter 上跑了 36.8T token。OpenAI、Google、Anthropic、xAI 四家加起来约 33T。

OpenRouter 现在的榜单方向也一致。最近 7 天，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 一个模型就跑了 33.6T，GPT-6 Luna 是 6.46T。

但再看请求数。

DeepSeek 占 21.8%，Google 21.5%，OpenAI 18.2%，Anthropic 2.5%。

光后三家加起来就有 42.2%，接近 DeepSeek 两倍。

所以我觉得这张图真正说明的，更像是 DeepSeek 正在吃下大量高 token 的 Agent 工作负载。长上下文、多轮执行、工具调用一跑起来，token 很容易堆上去。

OpenRouter 自己此前也观察到，DeepSeek token 份额的增长主要由 Agent 场景推动。

而且 OpenRouter 也写得很清楚，token 不等于用户数、请求数或收入，不同模型的 tokenisation 也不同。

Claude、GPT 还有大量流量直接走官方渠道，本来就不会出现在这里。

所以「DeepSeek 全面超过美国模型」我觉得说过头了。

但另一个信号已经很明显了。

在价格敏感、Token 消耗巨大的 Agent 场景里，便宜又够用的 Flash 模型正在快速吃量。

posts.text:
The real world abounds with recursively self-improving systems, but one in particular deserves attention: Science, modeled as a system (perhaps even as an agent, with goals and resources). If you want to really understand AI RSI, science should be your reference point.

Science is an intelligent system, and it is obviously recursively self-improving:

1. Scientific discoveries unlock new technology that helps build better experimental tools. This is a top driver of progress in nearly all fields.
2. They unlock new conceptual advances (ideas, theories) that help solve more problems.
3. They increase society's economic output, leading to more resources flowing into science.
4. They unlock better faster tooling (e.g. more compute via better chip & networking technology).

As a result, many measures of scientific *input* grow exponentially:

1. Headcount (doubles every ~15 years)
2. Global R&D spending (doubles a bit faster, every ~13 years)
3. Papers and patents (technically this is a measure of headcount)
4. Compute dedicated to science (doubles every ~2 years)

But is scientific progress exponential? Historically, the rate of scientific impact over time has remained roughly constant since the start of the industrial revolution (i.e. scientific progress is *linear*). 1850-1900 was about as dramatic as 1900-1950 or 1950-2000.

1850–1900: Evolution, germ theory & antiseptic surgery, thermodynamics, electromagnetic field equations, the periodic table, pharmaceuticals, electricity, telegraph and telephone, internal combustion engine, skyscrapers, mechanized agriculture...

1900–1950: special and general relativity, quantum mechanics, nuclear fission & atomic energy, antibiotics, genetic theory, electronic computers, information theory, synthetic polymers and plastics, the transistor, aviation...

1950–2000: DNA, genetic engineering, integrated circuits, microprocessors & personal computing, the Internet, crewed spaceflight, moon landing, satellite communications & GPS, standard model of particle physics...

In real terms, like life expectancy, which has increased in a remarkably linear fashion of roughly 3 months per year since 1840, progress is a straight line. This is especially apparent for fields where impact is easy to measure, like biology, medicine, and agriculture.

I first wrote about this phenomenon and its causes in 2012, and a steady stream of research has confirmed it in the years since. Examples include the 2018 paper by Nielsen and Collison, "Science Is Getting Less Bang for Its Buck," and the 2020 economic paper, "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?" (In fact, I believe the Nielsen paper stemmed from a conversation I had with him about this exact idea six months earlier)

In short, the primary cause is that research solves the highest-impact, easiest problems first, and every subsequent problem is either harder or lower-impact. Exponentially so. The paper that presented information theory wasn't very hard to write (single author!) but you'd have a hard time ever writing a CS paper that beats it in impact.

This is why science as a system requires exponential resources (input) to produce linear impact (output). It gets exponentially harder over time.

Worth thinking about if you're pondering RSI for AI. I fully believe AI RSI is already happening and will accelerate in the future. But I do not believe this leads to an "intelligence explosion" -- that would fly in the face of everything I know about intelligence and everything I know about recursively self-improving systems.

expert.name: Francois Chollet
expert.why: AGI 评测、抽象能力、推理基准

editorial.evidence: 科研投入指数增长产出线性
editorial.rationale: 有研究论据但偏理论观点

posts.translationZh:
现实世界中充满了递归式自我改进系统，但其中一个尤其值得关注：科学，作为一个系统来建模（甚至可以视为一个拥有目标和资源的智能体）。如果你想真正理解 AI 的递归式自我改进，科学应该是你的参照点。

科学是一个智能系统，而且显然是递归式自我改进的：

1. 科学发现解锁新技术，帮助制造更好的实验工具。这是几乎所有领域进步的主要驱动力之一。
2. 它们解锁新的概念进展（思想、理论），帮助解决更多问题。
3. 它们提升社会经济产出，使更多资源流向科学。
4. 它们解锁更好、更快的工具（例如通过更好的芯片和网络技术获得更多计算能力）。

因此，许多科学“投入”指标都呈指数增长：

1. 研究人员数量（约每 15 年翻一番）
2. 全球研发支出（翻番稍快，约每 13 年）
3. 论文和专利（严格说这是人员数量的一个指标）
4. 投入科学的计算资源（约每 2 年翻一番）

但科学进步是指数级的吗？从历史上看，自工业革命以来，科学影响力随时间变化的速率大致保持恒定（也就是说，科学进步是线性的）。1850-1900 年的变化，与 1900-1950 年或 1950-2000 年差不多同样剧烈。

1850–1900：进化论、细菌理论和抗菌手术、热力学、电磁场方程、元素周期表、制药、电力、电报和电话、内燃机、摩天大楼、机械化农业……

1900–1950：狭义和广义相对论、量子力学、核裂变和原子能、抗生素、遗传理论、电子计算机、信息论、合成聚合物和塑料、晶体管、航空……

1950–2000：DNA、基因工程、集成电路、微处理器和个人计算、互联网、载人航天、登月、卫星通信和 GPS、粒子物理标准模型……

从实际指标来看，比如预期寿命，自 1840 年以来一直以每年约 3 个月的惊人线性方式增长，进步就是一条直线。在生物学、医学和农业等影响容易衡量的领域，这一点尤其明显。

我最早在 2012 年写过这个现象及其成因，此后多年持续有研究证实它。例子包括 Nielsen 和 Collison 2018 年的论文《Science Is Getting Less Bang for Its Buck》，以及 2020 年的经济学论文《Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?》（事实上，我相信 Nielsen 那篇论文源于我六个月前和他关于这个确切想法的一次谈话）

简而言之，主要原因是研究会先解决影响最大、最容易的问题，而之后的每一个问题要么更难，要么影响更小。并且是指数级地如此。提出信息论的那篇论文并不难写（单作者！），但你几乎不可能再写出一篇影响力超过它的 CS 论文。

这就是为什么科学作为一个系统，需要指数级资源（投入）才能产生线性影响（产出）。它会随着时间变得指数级更难。

如果你在思考 AI 的递归式自我改进，这一点值得考虑。我完全相信 AI 的递归式自我改进已经在发生，并且未来会加速。但我不认为这会导致“智能爆炸”——那会违背我对智能的全部理解，也违背我对递归式自我改进系统的全部理解。

我们是不是高估了 Harness 对 Coding Agent「能力」的提升？

这篇论文中把模型固定，只替换 Claude Code、mini-SWE-agent 和 OpenCode，在 SWE-bench Verified 上重新测试。

结果很有意思。

在 447 个任务上，最重的 Claude Code 和最轻的 mini-SWE-agent，成绩差异落在 5 个百分点以内。

在 45 个高难任务、5 个模型上，换 Harness 会让 13% 的任务结果发生变化；但什么都不改，只把同一个配置再跑一遍，同样有 13% 的任务会翻转。

也就是说，很多看起来像 Harness 带来的提升，可能还没有明显超过运行本身的随机波动。

真正拉开差距的反而是成本。

同一个模型、同一批任务，不同 Harness 的单任务成本最高能差 3 倍。主要原因很简单：系统 Prompt 和工具 schema 会在每一步重复进入上下文，初始开销再被执行步数不断放大。

论文还提醒了一个容易被忽略的问题：

45 个任务连 13 个百分点的差距都只有约一半概率能检出；即使做到 447 个任务，分辨率也大约只有 5 个百分点。

所以我们得把 Harness 的价值拆开看了。

它当然会影响 Agent 怎么工作，但很多时候，最稳定、最容易测出来的差异，可能先体现在 token、成本和执行效率上。

这两天刷屏的「DeepSeek 一家 token 量超过美国四家总和」，我去 OpenRouter 官方榜单核了一下。

按 token 算，基本属实；换成请求数看，故事就完全不一样了。

Social Capital 统计的 9 月最后一周，DeepSeek 在 OpenRouter 上跑了 36.8T token。OpenAI、Google、Anthropic、xAI 四家加起来约 33T。

OpenRouter 现在的榜单方向也一致。最近 7 天，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 一个模型就跑了 33.6T，GPT-6 Luna 是 6.46T。

但再看请求数。

DeepSeek 占 21.8%，Google 21.5%，OpenAI 18.2%，Anthropic 2.5%。

光后三家加起来就有 42.2%，接近 DeepSeek 两倍。

所以我觉得这张图真正说明的，更像是 DeepSeek 正在吃下大量高 token 的 Agent 工作负载。长上下文、多轮执行、工具调用一跑起来，token 很容易堆上去。

OpenRouter 自己此前也观察到，DeepSeek token 份额的增长主要由 Agent 场景推动。

而且 OpenRouter 也写得很清楚，token 不等于用户数、请求数或收入，不同模型的 tokenisation 也不同。

Claude、GPT 还有大量流量直接走官方渠道，本来就不会出现在这里。

所以「DeepSeek 全面超过美国模型」我觉得说过头了。

但另一个信号已经很明显了。

在价格敏感、Token 消耗巨大的 Agent 场景里，便宜又够用的 Flash 模型正在快速吃量。

reviewedPosts.author: fchollet
reviewedPosts.text:
The real world abounds with recursively self-improving systems, but one in particular deserves attention: Science, modeled as a system (perhaps even as an agent, with goals and resources). If you want to really understand AI RSI, science should be your reference point.

Science is an intelligent system, and it is obviously recursively self-improving:

1. Scientific discoveries unlock new technology that helps build better experimental tools. This is a top driver of progress in nearly all fields.
2. They unlock new conceptual advances (ideas, theories) that help solve more problems.
3. They increase society's economic output, leading to more resources flowing into science.
4. They unlock better faster tooling (e.g. more compute via better chip & networking technology).

As a result, many measures of scientific *input* grow exponentially:

1. Headcount (doubles every ~15 years)
2. Global R&D spending (doubles a bit faster, every ~13 years)
3. Papers and patents (technically this is a measure of headcount)
4. Compute dedicated to science (doubles every ~2 years)

But is scientific progress exponential? Historically, the rate of scientific impact over time has remained roughly constant since the start of the industrial revolution (i.e. scientific progress is *linear*). 1850-1900 was about as dramatic as 1900-1950 or 1950-2000.

1850–1900: Evolution, germ theory & antiseptic surgery, thermodynamics, electromagnetic field equations, the periodic table, pharmaceuticals, electricity, telegraph and telephone, internal combustion engine, skyscrapers, mechanized agriculture...

1900–1950: special and general relativity, quantum mechanics, nuclear fission & atomic energy, antibiotics, genetic theory, electronic computers, information theory, synthetic polymers and plastics, the transistor, aviation...

1950–2000: DNA, genetic engineering, integrated circuits, microprocessors & personal computing, the Internet, crewed spaceflight, moon landing, satellite communications & GPS, standard model of particle physics...

In real terms, like life expectancy, which has increased in a remarkably linear fashion of roughly 3 months per year since 1840, progress is a straight line. This is especially apparent for fields where impact is easy to measure, like biology, medicine, and agriculture.

I first wrote about this phenomenon and its causes in 2012, and a steady stream of research has confirmed it in the years since. Examples include the 2018 paper by Nielsen and Collison, "Science Is Getting Less Bang for Its Buck," and the 2020 economic paper, "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?" (In fact, I believe the Nielsen paper stemmed from a conversation I had with him about this exact idea six months earlier)

In short, the primary cause is that research solves the highest-impact, easiest problems first, and every subsequent problem is either harder or lower-impact. Exponentially so. The paper that presented information theory wasn't very hard to write (single author!) but you'd have a hard time ever writing a CS paper that beats it in impact.

This is why science as a system requires exponential resources (input) to produce linear impact (output). It gets exponentially harder over time.

Worth thinking about if you're pondering RSI for AI. I fully believe AI RSI is already happening and will accelerate in the future. But I do not believe this leads to an "intelligence explosion" -- that would fly in the face of everything I know about intelligence and everything I know about recursively self-improving systems.
